claims.text: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coatings exhibit enhanced creep resistance when they contain heterogeneous phase boundaries.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Heat treatment or alloying adjustments can be used to increase or decrease FCC/BCC phase-boundary density.
Thermally activated creep operates within the proposed test-temperature regime.
The proposed conditions can remain below those causing dynamic recovery or significant microstructural coarsening.
Solute segregation may enhance the ability of FCC/BCC interfaces to impede dislocation motion.
Lattice mismatch at FCC/BCC phase boundaries impedes dislocations generated during continuous loading.
Solute-enriched phase boundaries impede dislocations generated during continuous loading.
Impeded dislocation motion produces a reduced rate of plastic deformation.
A high density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries will produce lower creep rates than a largely homogenized single-phase microstructure.
A high density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries will produce less accumulated plastic deformation than a largely homogenized single-phase microstructure.
Phase-boundary-controlled resistance is expected to dominate under sustained stress at moderate to high temperatures when significant grain growth and phase coarsening are absent.
Preliminary observations support dislocation pinning at phase boundaries.
